best_field_traits: INTRODUCED JAPANESE BROME: follow slender sometimes KINKED, arching panicle branches bearing several hanging AWNED MULTI-FLOWERED spikelets. At 10–20× count glume veins: lower commonly 3–5, upper often 7 (FNA); compare rare native Texas brome lower ONE and upper THREE. The awns on Japanese's individual lemmas can be twisted/divergent. Panicle droop and awn color alone never prove ID.
GENUS: Bromus PANICLES carry MULTI-FLOWERED spikelets; outer pair = GLUMES, inner overlapping units = LEMMAS, often with AWNS; not a true Hordeum/Elymus rachis SPIKE.
Cool-season winter annual, generally with soft or shaggy lower leaf sheaths and no persistent perennial crown.
Open panicle 8–20 cm, slender flexuous branches whose tips often droop or bend/kink.
Mature spikelets with about 6–12 florets; Oklahoma State gives 15–25 mm while FNA describes 20–40 mm, so use glume veins, lemma characters and awns rather than a single length cutoff.
Fertile lemma generally ~7–9 mm long with a divergent often twisted/bent ~8–13 mm awn; inspect 2–3 attached florets.
Rescuegrass B. catharticus is COMPARISON ONLY: large BROAD FLATTENED spikelets with short or no awns; many awned bromes differ from it.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Japanese brome — Bromus japonicus: Introduced cool-season annual. Usually small-to-moderate narrow awned spikelets on flexible, often nodding/kinked panicle branches. Flora of North America typically gives lower glume 3–5 veins, upper 7 veins; separate from native Texas brome's 1/3-veined pair. Lanceolate brome — Bromus lanceolatus: Introduced annual. Typically larger long lance-shaped spikelets ~25–50 mm, with roughly 8–20 florets and ~12–18 mm mature lemmas; open panicle. Hairy woodland brome — Bromus pubescens: Native North American woodland perennial, often taller with broader soft leaves, and open drooping panicle. Shorter generally straight lemma awns commonly 3–8 mm. Lower glume typically 1-veined; true pubescence may be obvious on entire lemma. Texas brome — Bromus texensis: Texas-native annual restricted to limited Texas sites. Flora of North America: often 20–30 mm spikelets with 4–7 florets, lower glume ONE vein (~6–9 mm), upper THREE (~8–10.5 mm), lemma ~9–15 mm and awn ~4–8 mm. Rescuegrass — Bromus catharticus (comparison only): Introduced South American cool-season grass, often annual or short-lived perennial depending ecology/treatment. Larger broad 16–40 mm strongly flattened spikelets, many florets and short/no awns (often 0–4 mm).

field_matrix.where_to_look: Measure an intact mature spikelet including ALL florets excluding its awns, then count fertile florets.
field_matrix.look_alike: Introduced annual. Typically larger long lance-shaped spikelets ~25–50 mm, with roughly 8–20 florets and ~12–18 mm mature lemmas; open panicle.
field_matrix.confirmation: Compare long often pointed spikelets with Japanese brome's often smaller fewer florets, but both dimensions vary; check true lemma body and awn attachment at 10–20×.
field_matrix.avoid_false_identification: Length alone overlaps rescuegrass and native bromes; always count florets and inspect glumes.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Use whole flowering panicle + intact mature multi-flowered spikelet measurements together.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Look at actual rooted crown, then hairy lemma surface at 10× and sheath/true collar.
field_matrix.look_alike: Native North American woodland perennial, often taller with broader soft leaves, and open drooping panicle. Shorter generally straight lemma awns commonly 3–8 mm. Lower glume typically 1-veined; true pubescence may be obvious on entire lemma.
field_matrix.confirmation: A mature persistent perennial tuft/crown and hairy lemmas support pubescens, unlike short-lived Japanese, lanceolate and Texas annuals.
field_matrix.avoid_false_identification: Hairy sheaths alone are NOT proof: multiple annual bromes have pubescent sheaths too. 389×589 archived source doesn't show lemma hairs.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Use whole flowering panicle + intact mature multi-flowered spikelet measurements together.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Measure mature spikelet, glumes and lemma at mm scale; count veins on BOTH persistent GLUMES.
field_matrix.look_alike: Texas-native annual restricted to limited Texas sites. Flora of North America: often 20–30 mm spikelets with 4–7 florets, lower glume ONE vein (~6–9 mm), upper THREE (~8–10.5 mm), lemma ~9–15 mm and awn ~4–8 mm.
field_matrix.confirmation: This 1/3 vein pair distinguishes from Japanese's commonly higher 3–5/7 vein counts. The lemma apex described as entire by FNA but sometimes toothed in other treatments: DO NOT force an ID from 'two teeth'.
field_matrix.avoid_false_identification: This is a botanically important native versus introduced split. Preserve TAXON/RANGE decisions and label uncertain lookalikes Bromus sp.; Hays County origin NOT proven from these photo references.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Inspect a mature INTACT glume pair and count actual longitudinal veins, not awns or background photos.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Whole flowering panicle: look for big FLAT, broad, oat-like spikelets with very SHORT or absent awns.
field_matrix.look_alike: Introduced South American cool-season grass, often annual or short-lived perennial depending ecology/treatment. Larger broad 16–40 mm strongly flattened spikelets, many florets and short/no awns (often 0–4 mm).
field_matrix.confirmation: Large flattened overlapping V/oat-like florets contrast with Japanese brome's narrow long-awned units and lanceolate brome's narrower long densely floret spikelets.
field_matrix.avoid_false_identification: Not installed in learner. Annual-versus-perennial is NOT sufficient: Texas A&M treats annual, Kew often perennial.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Use whole flowering panicle + intact mature multi-flowered spikelet measurements together.

not_reliable_alone: One awn length, purple seedhead color, or an overall nodding silhouette without attached spikelets.
Soft hair on lower SHEATH: found on multiple introduced and native Bromus species.
Whole head length alone: Flora of North America, Kew GrassBase and Texas regional treatments report overlapping but non-identical ranges.
Lower and upper glume vein count from a photograph that doesn't actually resolve the glumes under backlight.
Presence of yellow extruded ANTHERS: diagnostic of flowering grass stage, NOT Bromus texensis species.
An apparently perennial tuft when broken roots or mowing obscure annual/reproductive life cycle.
Unreviewed county nativity; rare native Texas brome may resemble introduced Japanese brome.

field_id_finish_pass.crew_teaching_summary: Cool-season INTRODUCED annual; slender, often kinked or drooping panicle branches carry several awned, multi-flowered spikelets. Published spikelet lengths overlap other Bromus species (Oklahoma State ~15–25 mm; FNA ~20–40 mm), so use mature glume veins and lemma/awn anatomy instead of a short size cutoff. Lower sheaths may be soft-haired.
field_id_finish_pass.lookalike_comparison: Compared to B. lanceolatus, usually shorter spikelets with fewer florets and more relaxed/kinked drooping branches; lanceolatus often has ~25–50 mm spikelets with 8–20 florets. Compared to native B. texensis, note Texas brome generally shorter 6–10 mm awns and requires lemma/branch dissection, not habitat alone. Unlike perennial B. pubescens, this is an annual and usually shorter-lived.

diagnostic_species_finalization_20261023.look_here_first: Introduced cool-season annual with loose, often drooping/kinked panicle branches and multi-flowered awned spikelets. Count florets and examine a detached mature lemma and BOTH glumes before deciding between Japanese, lanceolate, Texas, and woodland bromes.
diagnostic_species_finalization_20261023.growth_form: Fibrous-rooted annual, usually about 22–70 cm; no perennial rhizomatous crown. Lower sheaths often softly hairy, but sheath pubescence varies. Membranous ligule approximately 1–2.2 mm (Go Botany), not an awn or tuft of sheath hairs.
diagnostic_species_finalization_20261023.spikelet_glume_lemma_awn: Mature spikelets approximately 20–40 mm in Go Botany/FNA treatment, with usually 6–12 florets; other regional treatments report 15–25 mm. Lower glume body approximately 4.5–7 mm, upper 5–8 mm, glumes awnless; lower glume commonly 3–5-veined and upper often 7-veined. Fertile lemma body approximately 7–9 mm with one 8–13 mm awn often divergent or bent when dry; count glume veins under 10–20× and separate awn from lemma body.
diagnostic_species_finalization_20261023.lookalikes: Bromus lanceolatus often has longer, more many-flowered spikelets (approximately 25–50 mm and 8–20 florets), though ranges overlap. B. texensis typically has 1-veined lower and 3-veined upper glumes; B. pubescens is perennial, often woodland-associated, with short awns and hairy lemmas. B. catharticus has much broader, flattened spikelets and shorter/absent awns.

Flora of North America describes lemmas 9–15 mm long, an entire acute/subulate apex and a straight 4–8 mm awn inserted just below the tip. Compare mature lower/upper glumes (usually 1 and 3 veins), lemma length and awn with introduced Japanese and lanceolate bromes. Yellow flowering anthers are not species-specific; other treatments differ on tip terminology, so never force this identification from apparent teeth.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Japanese brome — first see the real spikelet, then measure
steps: START with the annotated ORIGINAL real photo. Follow a FLOWERING PANICLE branch to one MULTI-FLOWERED SPIKELET; each overlapping scale is a distinct lemma/floret, not one giant grain.
COLLECT a ripe intact spikelet with a 1-mm ruler. Identify two outer GLUMES, then the inner LEMMAS and any AWNS; count florets.
CHECK the hanging, often kinked fine panicle branches and flexible outward/twisted awns, but never decide native versus introduced from droop alone.
COMPARE all four installed Bromus photographs together. The broad-flat short-awn RESCUEGRASS is an external comparison ONLY.
If the mature two-glume/lemma structures are obscured or the source could be a scarce native brome, keep ID as Bromus sp. rather than assigning invasive management by silhouette.

SCALED LEMMA PHOTO NOW ON THIS PAGE: inspect the physically archived Stefan.lefnaer photograph with its real 5-mm source bar. Three arrows point to visible lemma surface, pale margin and awn; the two outer glumes and true ligule are not shown.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: For native versus introduced Bromus, the important structures are glume VEINS, actual lemma dimensions and awns, and an annual or perennial rooted crown—not the word 'brome' or a pretty nodding head.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Four exact-species JPEG records are physically archived in GitHub; three of the ten comparison panels (0–2) display archived Japanese brome, panels 3–7 show other bromes/rescuegrass, and panels 8–9 externally reference source-verified hairy nodes/sheaths (not a true ligule). Stefan.lefnaer's archived lemma/awn photo contains a genuine 5-mm scale and existing visible-structure arrows, but isolated glume vein counts, inner ligule, precise awn insertion, and a rooted Central Texas voucher are still missing. Preserve individual CC BY-NC / CC BY-SA rights and attribution. FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS; live site NOT VERIFIED.

what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Whole rooted native-range flowering plant to document annual versus perennial duration and habitat.
Entire mature panicle including every branch origin and 2–3 intact ripe spikelets with 1 cm scale.
Paired lower and upper GLUMES opened without damage: count longitudinal veins using backlight at 10–20× and 1-mm ruler.
Mature lemma with measured length and actual terminal tooth/apex shape plus exact origin and length of single lemma awn.
Cross-section or profile of spikelet to document broad flattened rescuegrass versus more narrow lanceolate type.
Lower leaf sheath HAIRS and true membranous LIGULE at blade–sheath collar, photographed on same plant.
Compare a confirmed Texas brome against local Japanese brome under same 1-mm ruler before invasive removal.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — INTRODUCED JAPANESE BROME
field_id_short_tiles.short: Annual with loose often nodding, kinked branches and awned, MULTIFLORED spikelets; confirm glume veins before removal.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Follow a complete panicle, not an isolated hanging spikelet. FNA describes an open 10–22 cm panicle with slender flexuous branches and mature spikelets often 20–40 mm with about 6–12 florets; other treatments report shorter 12–20 mm spikelets. These ranges overlap other bromes. Panels 0–2 show real Japanese brome reproductive material, but no current image alone establishes a Central Texas voucher or all key dimensions. A newly locally archived real Texas flowering-grassland photograph from Goldthwaite (panel 11, Sam Kieschnick CC BY) now adds field habit in its actual growing environment. The surrounding grass community is mixed, and the buried roots and exact complete crown-to-head physical connection are NOT shown; do not identify Japanese brome from green growth alone.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL TEXAS FIELD HABIT AND MATURE SPIKELETS PHOTOGRAPHED; EXTRACTED CONNECTED ROOT-TO-PANICLE PLANT STILL MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · ROOTED ANNUAL, SHEATH AND TRUE LIGULE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Actual hairy culm nodes/sheaths pictured; true ligule and rooted crown missing
field_id_short_tiles.details: Stefan.lefnaer's CC BY-SA 4.0 source-labelled Austrian original photos are now archived LOCALLY: panel 8 shows true red-brown nodes on hairy green culms with a real 5-mm scale; panel 9 documents hairy leaf sheaths and blade overlap. These pictures show the actual external tissues, not the short INSIDE free 1–2.2 mm membranous ligule. Roots are not exposed. Do not confuse a stem joint, sheath hair, or outer collar with a ligule. Next needed photograph: gently opened same-plant blade/sheath junction face-on with physical millimeter scale, plus continuous connected root-to-panicle evidence. Two more locally stored research-grade species-specific Texas photos now show the actual leaf/sheath exterior held in Rockdale (panel 12) and the lower blade insertion from Mills County (panel 13), both by Linda Jo Conn under individual CC BY licenses. They show exactly WHERE to look for the ligule on a true Japanese brome plant, not the verified 1–2 mm free INNER membranous flap. Panel 11 adds a grassland flowering growth context, but fibrous roots are still buried.
field_id_short_tiles.status: FOUR LOCAL TRUE HAIRY SHEATH/LEAF-COLLAR MACROS INCLUDING TWO TEXAS; FREE LIGULE EDGE AND CONNECTED ROOTS NOT CERTIFIED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · COUNT FLORETS AND GLUME VEINS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Usually 6–12 florets; lower glume commonly (3)5-veined, upper usually 7-veined.
field_id_short_tiles.details: At 10–20× backlight TWO persistent glumes at the BASE of a mature spikelet; do not count lemma veins as glume veins. FNA gives lower glume 4.5–7 mm, upper 5–8 mm, both awnless. Native Texas brome generally has ONE-veined lower and THREE-veined upper glume. Use three authenticated mature spikelets and 1-mm scale before making a confident invasive-versus-native distinction. NEW panel 10 NOW shows an authentic species-specific PAIR OF OUTER GLUMES from the BASE of Japanese brome spikelets, archived from Stefan.lefnaer's actual Austrian specimens (CC BY-SA 4.0). This is significant new photographic evidence for locating true glumes, but the two glume vein counts have NOT been independently resolved from these compressed pixels. Do not add veins or assume (3)5/7 by reading the nearby lemma photo. A calibrated backlit isolated pair remains a hold before removing plants mistaken for native Texas brome.
field_id_short_tiles.status: ACTUAL BASAL GLUME PAIR NOW PHOTOGRAPHED — LOWER / UPPER NERVE COUNTS NOT YET CERTIFIED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · LEMMA BODY, SUBAPICAL AWN AND DRYING TWIST
field_id_short_tiles.short: Fertile lemma about 7–9 mm; its one awn usually 8–13 mm and arises below the lemma tip.
field_id_short_tiles.details: The lemma is the bract around EACH floret, not an outer glume. FNA describes 7–9 mm lemma bodies, usually 8–13 mm awns arising at least about 1.5 mm below a shallowly bifid apex; awns often diverge or twist as they dry. Existing archived macro shows real lemma and awn outlines but is not a calibrated proof of insertion depth or the vein count. Preserve treatment differences in awn lengths and lemma tip descriptions.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL MACRO PRESENT — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO MEASURED AWN INSERTION

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES — DON'T REMOVE TEXAS BROME
field_id_short_tiles.short: Native Texas brome has typically 1/3-veined glumes; Japanese brome generally (3)5/7.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Comparison panel 3 is NATIVE Texas brome and is NOT a Japanese brome anatomy photo. Panel 4 is introduced lanceolate brome, often with much longer 25–50 mm spikelets and 8–20 florets. Panel 5 shows native woodland perennial B. pubescens, which can also have a 1/3-veined glume pair. Rescuegrass in panels 6–7 is a DIFFERENT species with broader flattened spikelets. Require actual glume venation, annual roots and lemma anatomy; never decide invasive removal by drooping heads alone.
field_id_short_tiles.status: NATIVE TEXAS BROME LOOK-ALIKE ARROWS SYNCHRONIZED; NEW JAPANESE GLUME-BASE IMAGE NOT CROSS-SPECIES SUBSTITUTE

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE — DIAGNOSTIC MACROS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Nine openly licensed Japanese brome species photos in teaching panels; roots, inside ligule and backlit glume nerves remain.
field_id_short_tiles.details: CANONICAL OCTOBER 27 REAL JAPANESE BROME PHOTOS: ten species-specific archived JPEG records, of which NINE have individually validated openly reusable licenses and appear in the Learner (three older actual mature spikelet/lemma photos, two new Austrian true hairy sheath/culm-node macros, an Austrian true basal-glume photograph, one actual Goldthwaite Texas plant in grassland, one Rockdale external sheath, and one Mills County external blade/collar junction). The tenth, older CC BY-NC iNaturalist image remains an archival research photo, NOT in the public teaching gallery. Fourteen gallery panels total = NINE real Japanese brome photo panels and FIVE OTHER species lookalike panels, two of them still externally served rescuegrass. All six new source images in this pass were physically archived and linked locally, with source creator/photo licenses and image hashes; new images did not receive unsupported anatomical arrows. The native Texas brome comparison uses its corrected canonical markers. ESTIMATED photographic role completeness ~67% (4/6 six-role equivalent): clear reproductive lemma/awn, glume BASE visible but independent vein counts unmeasured, true hairy sheath photographs and outside collar, in-ground Texas live habit with hidden roots, comparisons, and source-labelled panicle recognition. Not fully public-ready: true face-on free 1–2.2 mm ligule, pulled connected fibrous crown-to-head specimen, and individually counted backlit Japanese (3)5/7 versus native Texas 1/3 glume nerves with real 1-mm ruler are missing. Live GitHub Pages deployment and mobile arrows remain unchecked. No extra invasive-removal proof is inferred from head shape.
